hints: Focus on what actually controls the forward rate, not just the position of equilibrium. Remember rate depends on concentration.
Write the forward rate expression as rate = k[H2][I2] and ask yourself which changes raise the concentrations of H2 and I2 at the new equilibrium.
Compare adding inert gas at constant volume with adding HI or compressing the syringe, and check which two leave you with more reactant particles per unit volume once equilibrium is re-established.
walkthrough:
**Recall what makes the forward rate bigger**

Think like a kinetics person first. For $\text{H}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{HI}(g)$ the forward rate depends on the reactants.

$$\text{forward rate} = k_f[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]$$
So the question is really asking, in which new equilibrium are $[\text{H}_2]$ and $[\text{I}_2]$ higher than before?

**Test change 1, inert gas at constant volume**

Adding inert gas raises total pressure but it does not change the partial pressures or concentrations of $\text{H}_2$, $\text{I}_2$ or $\text{HI}$ because volume is fixed.

$$[\text{X}] = n_{\text{X}} / V \text{ unchanged}$$
No change in concentrations means no change in rates and no shift in equilibrium. So 1 does nothing.

**Test change 2, add product HI at constant volume**

Adding $\text{HI}$ instantly raises $[\text{HI}]$, so $Q_c > K_c$ where:
$$Q_c = \frac{[\text{HI}]^2}{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]}$$
The system shifts left to use up some of the added $\text{HI}$, making more $\text{H}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$. At the new equilibrium both $[\text{H}_2]$ and $[\text{I}_2]$ are higher than originally, so $k_f[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]$ is larger. So 2 counts.

**Test change 3, decrease volume by pushing piston**

Halving volume (for example) doubles every concentration at once. Both forward and reverse rates jump up because collisions are more frequent.

$$\text{moles gas left = 2, right = 2, so no shift in mole ratio}$$
Because $\Delta n = 0$, the position does not shift to one side, but all equilibrium concentrations are now higher in the smaller volume. Higher $[\text{H}_2]$ and $[\text{I}_2]$ means a higher forward rate. So 3 counts.

Together, 2 and 3 give an increased forward rate.

options.A: 2 only is incomplete. Adding HI does increase [H2] and [I2] after a left shift, so the forward rate does increase, but change 3 also increases it. You would miss the effect of compression.
options.B: 1 and 2 is wrong because 1 is a classic trap. Adding inert gas at constant volume does not change partial pressures or concentrations, so rates and equilibrium position are unchanged.
options.C: 1 and 3 is wrong because it includes the inert gas change. Change 3 is correct since smaller volume means higher [H2] and [I2] and faster forward rate, but change 1 has no effect.
options.D: 2 and 3 is correct. In 2, added HI shifts equilibrium left, producing extra H2 and I2, so equilibrium [H2][I2] is higher. In 3, compression raises all concentrations with no shift (equal moles), so equilibrium [H2][I2] is higher. Both give a larger forward rate = kf[H2][I2].
